analogy.p: Imagine the audience given the feed from a camera inside Macbeth's head. We see every flicker of doubt before the crime and every hardening after it, while the characters in the room see only his face. Dramatic irony is the gap between the feed and the room. The analogy breaks down because a camera records passively, whereas Macbeth's soliloquies are rhetoric: they are shaped, performed and persuasive, so we should ask what he wants us to feel.
analogy.t: A security camera in the villain's head

bullets: A soliloquy shows the **truth** of a character's thinking because there is no one to lie to. Even a liar like Lady Macbeth is honest with herself in 1.5.
An aside reveals instant reactions. Macbeth's asides in 1.3 and 1.4 show ambition surfacing while he is still publicly loyal.
Overheard speech (Lady Macbeth sleepwalking in 5.1) is a variation: the speaker is unaware, so the confession is involuntary.
The effect is double: **sympathy** (we understand his fear and imagination) and **complicity** (we are told the plot and cannot stop it).
Because the audience is ahead of the stage characters, nearly every public scene carries **dramatic irony**.

callouts.p: A speech in which a character, alone on stage, speaks private thoughts aloud to the audience.
A remark spoken to the audience or to oneself that other characters on stage are assumed not to hear.
When the audience knows something that one or more characters on stage do not, giving their words or actions a second meaning.

core.h: Definitions and the function of direct address
core.p: A **soliloquy** is a speech made by a character alone on stage, voicing private thoughts aloud. An **aside** is a short remark made to the audience, or to oneself, while other characters are present but supposedly cannot hear. Both are conventions of Elizabethan and Jacobean theatre, where the audience stood or sat very close to the actors, and both give the audience information that the other characters lack. In a tragedy about a murderer, this is a daring choice: we are made to spend time inside the mind of a man we should condemn.

bullets: **Act 1 Scene 3:** he says two truths are told, like happy prologues to the swelling act. The theatrical metaphor (prologue, act) shows he is thinking of his life as a drama he could write himself.
**Act 1 Scene 3:** this supernatural soliciting cannot be ill, cannot be good. The balanced, contradictory phrasing shows genuine uncertainty. He reasons both ways and ends in suspense.

**Act 1 Scene 3:** he is frightened by thoughts whose murder is yet fantastical, which shakes so his single state of man. The word murder appears before any plan: the idea has entered his mind and unsettles his whole identity.
**Act 1 Scene 3:** if chance will have me king, why, chance may crown me without my stir. This is a hopeful aside, a way out of guilt, because chance would do the work.

**Act 1 Scene 4:** after Duncan names Malcolm as heir, Macbeth says the Prince of Cumberland is a step he must fall down or o'erleap. Then comes Stars, hide your fires. The imagery turns from hesitation to a prayer for concealment.

callouts.p: Notice that Macbeth's first asides come immediately after the prophecy is confirmed. The structure makes the audience conscious that ambition is released by temptation, and it makes the later soliloquy of 1.7 feel like a considered argument.

core.p: Macbeth's first asides come in 1.3 after the witches have vanished. Ross and Angus arrive and announce that he is Thane of Cawdor, so the first prophecy has come true. While Banquo and the others talk, Macbeth speaks apart. The asides show a man whose mind is already racing and whose imagination is more powerful than his reason.

What Macbeth says (key phrase)
Effect
rows: Theatre metaphor; he begins to script his future
cannot be ill, cannot be good
Balanced syntax shows uncertainty; audience shares his dilemma
Thought threatens his identity; imagination stronger than will
Apostrophe; secret ambition now wishes to hide from heaven

bullets: It begins with a conditional: if it were done when 'tis done. The rhythm of repeated done and the monosyllables show a man circling a thought he hardly dares to say.
The legal and moral reasons (kinsman, subject, host) show that he knows the act is a betrayal of the social order and hospitality.

The pictures he uses (pity as a naked new-born babe striding the blast; Duncan's virtues pleading like angels) bring in innocence and divine judgement, and make the murder feel like an offence against heaven.
He admits he has no spur but only vaulting ambition, which o'erleaps itself. The horse-riding metaphor shows ambition as reckless and self-destructive, and he knows it will fall.
The speech breaks off mid-sentence, with the image of falling on th' other, as Lady Macbeth enters. She finishes his thought for him, and takes control of the next scene.

callouts.p: The 1.7 soliloquy proves Macbeth is not simply evil. He sees clearly and chooses wrongly, which is the definition of a tragic flaw operating in a free agent (hamartia).
Do not say he is persuaded by Lady Macbeth alone. The soliloquy shows his own ambition is the only spur he can name; she reinforces rather than creates it.

core.h: The soliloquy of 1.7: a mind arguing against its own plan
core.p: In 1.7 Macbeth leaves the feast and speaks alone. This is the most important soliloquy for his moral conflict because he lists every reason not to kill Duncan: he is a kinsman, a subject, a host, and Duncan is a virtuous king. The reasoning is rational, then emotional, and finally collapses into a confession of what drives him. Shakespeare ends the speech mid-sentence when Lady Macbeth enters, as if the argument had been interrupted by the very pressure he is trying to resist.

bullets: **Act 2 Scene 1:** is this a dagger which I see before me. The question form, the hallucination and the later admission that it is a dagger of the mind show his imagination turning against him. The scene ends with a rhyming couplet about a bell that summons Duncan to heaven or to hell, giving the act a ritual feel.

**Act 3 Scene 1:** to be thus is nothing; but to be safely thus. Banquo is now the threat, so the soliloquy is about security, not conscience. He says he has given his eternal jewel to the common enemy of man (the devil), and he does so only to make Banquo's sons kings, a bitter irony.

**Act 4 Scene 1:** the firstlings of my hand. Impulse replaces deliberation, and the plan to kill Macduff's family follows. This closing speech is shorter and harder than the earlier ones, with no imagery of doubt (it is spoken as an aside, with Lennox on stage).

**Act 5 Scene 5:** she should have died hereafter. The opening short line leaves silence, so the news of Lady Macbeth's death is met with a pause. Tomorrow, and tomorrow, and tomorrow creeps in a slow repeated rhythm, life is a walking shadow and a poor player, and a tale told by an idiot, full of sound and fury.

The 5.5 speech uses theatrical metaphor again (player, stage), echoing the two truths are told prologue of 1.3. The patterning shows he has gone from scripting his life to seeing it as meaningless performance.

core.h: The dagger soliloquy and the later speeches (Acts 2-5)
core.p: After 1.7 the soliloquies track his decline. In 2.1 he sees a dagger in the air and asks if it is a dagger of the mind, a false creation. In 3.1 he is king and wants to be safely so. In the closing speech of 4.1 he promises that the firstlings of his heart shall be the firstlings of his hand, which means he will act on impulse without conscience. In 5.5 he hears of his wife's death and gives the bleakest speech in the play. Each speech replaces a layer of imagination or doubt with something harder.

bullets: **Act 1 Scene 5:** milk of human kindness. She uses the imagery of nursing to describe weakness, linking kindness with femininity, which she then wants to reject by being unsexed.
**Act 1 Scene 5:** unsex me here. The imperative verb orders spirits to remove her gender, because in her view cruelty is masculine.

**Act 5 Scene 1:** she speaks in prose, in her sleep, in front of the Doctor and Gentlewoman. Out, damned spot. Her earlier control has failed; the private thoughts of 1.5 are now public and fragmented.
The structural symmetry is vital: after her brief private words at the start of 3.2 she never again addresses the audience alone, so we lose her as a confidante, and the couple drift apart.

callouts.p: Macbeth moves from private doubt to public hardness; Lady Macbeth moves from private hardness to public collapse. The reversal is a major structural point.

core.h: Lady Macbeth: private speech and the break in control
core.p: Lady Macbeth's soliloquy in 1.5 follows her reading of Macbeth's letter. She says that she fears his nature is too full of the milk of human kindness, then calls on spirits to unsex her. Her speech is the mirror of Macbeth's asides: where he fears his thoughts, she commands hers. The fact that the audience hears this before she meets Macbeth makes the later scene dramatic irony as well, since he hears her only in persuasion and we hear her in prayer.

bullets: **Act 1 Scene 4:** Duncan says there is no art to find the mind's construction in the face, and says he built an absolute trust on the executed Cawdor. Macbeth enters at that moment. Duncan then trusts the next Cawdor.

**Act 1 Scene 6:** Duncan describes the castle as having a pleasant seat. The gentle imagery of the temple-haunting martlet suggests safety, while the audience knows the Macbeths have decided to murder him that night.
**Act 3 Scene 4:** Macbeth toasts our dear friend Banquo, whom he knows is dead. The ghost returns at once, so his words seem to summon it.
**Act 4 Scene 2:** Lady Macduff and her son talk in a domestic scene. The son defiantly calls the murderer a shag-hair'd villain, and the audience knows he is about to die.
**Act 5 Scene 1:** Lady Macbeth earlier said a little water clears us of this deed, so her struggle to wash her hands is the cruellest irony of the play.

callouts.p: It makes the audience feel dread (we know what is coming), pity (innocents like Duncan and the Macduffs are unaware), and moral involvement (we have been trusted with the secret).

core.h: Dramatic irony: the audience knows more
core.p: Dramatic irony is not limited to soliloquies. Because the audience knows what Macbeth plans, many public speeches are loaded with a second meaning. The audience also knew the history and the legend of Banquo's descendants from the Jacobean point of view, so some irony relied on knowing what would happen in the future. Examiners reward students who explain how irony creates tension, not just those who label it.

bullets: Soliloquies make the audience a confidant, so we are implicated in the secret.
Because we hear his doubt, his later hardness feels like a loss. The dwindling imagination in 5.5 is moving precisely because we saw the rich imagination of 2.1.
The Jacobean audience would also have been conscious of King James, a monarch who survived the Gunpowder Plot, so the sight of a would-be regicide inside his own head was uneasy.
An alternative reading: soliloquy might not create sympathy at all but reveal how easily self-justification works.

callouts.p: End a paragraph with a judgement about the audience's response, such as: the soliloquy forces the audience to see Macbeth's conscience before it fades.

core.p: Shakespeare's use of soliloquy creates a complicated moral response. We know Macbeth is a murderer, yet we hear him explain his fear. This invites sympathy without removing judgement, so the audience is both horrified and moved. The same technique means Macbeth cannot become a pure villain, which is essential to the genre of tragedy, in which a great man falls through a flaw we understand.

bullets: Say where the speech falls: before or after the murder, before or after a prophecy.
Look at syntax: questions, conditionals, broken sentences, short lines.
Use the verbs reveals, conveys, exposes, confides, implicates.
Compare two speeches to show a change.
Link to context: the divine right of kings made a murderer's inner voice a risky subject.

callouts.p: Do not write: this is a soliloquy so it shows his thoughts. Say what the thoughts are, how the language shows them, and why the audience needs them.

core.p: A grade 9 paragraph will do three things: identify the speech type and its position in the play, analyse key words and rhythm, and explain the effect on the audience. Edexcel part (a) asks about an extract, so the focus should be on how the passage works, while part (b) asks for recall, so learn short key phrases with their Act and Scene.

plan: The Act 1 asides: ambition arrives faster than reason
The soliloquy of 1.7: the fullest debate and its interruption
The dagger of 2.1: imagination becomes the weapon
The decline of the later speeches to 5.5
Conclusion: soliloquy creates both complicity and tragedy
essays.q: How does Shakespeare use soliloquy to present Macbeth's ambition and conflict?
essays.text:
Shakespeare lets us into Macbeth's mind before he commits any crime, and the effect is to make ambition seem less like a decision than an infection. In the asides of Act 1 Scene 3, the conditional phrase two truths are told casts the witches' prophecies as happy prologues, a theatrical metaphor in which Macbeth already imagines himself as the author of a drama. Yet in the same scene he is frightened by a thought whose murder is yet fantastical, and this fear shakes his single state of man. The audience hears the word murder before anyone has planned it. This is Shakespeare's first strategy: asides make us confidants of an idea that the characters on stage cannot see.

The soliloquy of Act 1 Scene 7 is the heart of this process. Macbeth begins with the conditional if it were done when 'tis done, the repeated done circling the act without naming it, and then lists legal and moral reasons for restraint: he is Duncan's kinsman, subject and host. When he declares that he has no spur but only vaulting ambition, the metaphor casts ambition as a rider who overshoots, so Macbeth predicts his own fall in the language of a horse accident. The structural detail that matters most is the interruption: the sentence breaks off as Lady Macbeth enters, as if his private argument cannot survive contact with her pressure. Although it could be argued that she persuades him, the soliloquy shows that the only spur he can find is his own ambition. Lady Macbeth supplies the push; Macbeth supplies the direction.

In Act 2 Scene 1 the soliloquy moves from argument to vision. Is this a dagger which I see before me asks a question that no one answers, and the vision of gouts of blood on the blade (guilt arriving before the deed) shows his imagination turning against him. By calling it a dagger of the mind, he separates imagination from action, but he cannot stop. The speech ends with a rhyming couplet about a bell that summons Duncan to heaven or to hell, a ritual flourish that presents the murder as a kind of ceremony. A Jacobean audience, believing that evil spirits could deceive the mind, might have read the dagger as supernatural, though a modern audience may prefer a psychological reading.

After the murder the soliloquies become shorter and harder. In Act 3 Scene 1, to be thus is nothing but to be safely thus. The adverb safely reveals that he has the crown but not peace, and the eternal jewel given to the common enemy of man (the devil) shows that he understands the spiritual cost. By Act 4 Scene 1 he resolves that the firstlings of his heart shall be the firstlings of his hand, with no reflection left at all. Finally, in Act 5 Scene 5, she should have died hereafter begins with a short line that leaves a gap on stage, and tomorrow, and tomorrow, and tomorrow creeps in a slow repeated rhythm. Life becomes a poor player that struts and frets, a tale told by an idiot. The theatre imagery that began in 1.3 has come full circle, but now the drama is meaningless.

Soliloquy therefore makes the audience complicit in the story and then forces us to feel what has been lost. If the asides show an imagination excited by possibility, the final speech shows an imagination emptied of it. Shakespeare's purpose seems to be to make us pity a man whose crimes we condemn, and so to show that tragedy is the destruction of a mind we have understood.
essays.thesis: Shakespeare uses soliloquy not to excuse Macbeth but to make the audience witness the moment when a conscience is overruled by its own imagination, so that his later emptiness feels like a loss we have watched happen.
why: AO1: a conceptual thesis (conscience overruled by imagination) tracked across the play with short embedded quotations.
AO2: close attention to syntax (conditional, interrupted sentence, short line), metaphor (vaulting, dagger of the mind) and the structural echo of theatre imagery.
AO3: context woven into interpretation (Jacobean belief in deceiving spirits), with an alternative reading (psychological versus supernatural).
Evaluates the audience's response and the writer's purpose in the conclusion.

mistakes.r: Explain that they reveal inner conflict and shape our moral response to the character.
mistakes.w: Saying soliloquies are used to tell the audience the plot.

mistakes.r: Use the correct term: asides happen with others present; soliloquies are spoken alone.
mistakes.w: Confusing an aside with a soliloquy.

mistakes.r: Use the 1.7 soliloquy to show a man who understands the moral cost and chooses ambition.
mistakes.w: Saying Macbeth is evil from the start.

mistakes.r: Say what the audience knows, what the character believes, and what tension it creates.
mistakes.w: Labelling dramatic irony without explaining it.

mistakes.r: Use 1.5 and 5.1 as a symmetrical pair that shows a reversal of control.
Analyse the question form, hallucination, and the effect on the audience of seeing his mind fail to separate imagination from reality.
mistakes.w: Retelling what Macbeth says in the dagger speech.

mistakes.r: Use short phrases (vaulting ambition, the firstlings of my hand) accurately with their Act and Scene.

quotes.a: Macbeth describes the witches' predictions as happy prologues to the swelling act of the imperial theme. The theatrical metaphor shows him imagining his future as a script he could write. It reveals ambition before conscience has spoken, and sets up the play's theatre imagery that culminates in 5.5.
quotes.c: Jacobean audiences knew the theatrical convention of aside.

quotes.a: The balanced syntax of ill and good shows Macbeth's uncertainty. He reasons both ways without resolving, which makes the audience share his dilemma. The doubled negative form mimics a mind that cannot settle, and it foreshadows the equivocal nature of the witches' words.
quotes.c: Witches as ambiguous supernatural figures in Jacobean belief.
quotes.q: cannot be ill, cannot be good

quotes.a: The phrase suggests that a man is a unified kingdom, and that his thought of murder shakes the whole self. It turns inner conflict into a political metaphor, linked to the play's idea that regicide disrupts both the state and the individual.
quotes.c: Microcosm and macrocosm: the body and the state mirrored each other.

quotes.a: Macbeth addresses the stars, using apostrophe and an imperative. He is speaking to heaven as if it can be commanded, and his wish to hide his desires shows he already knows they are black and deep. It links his private conflict to the darkness pattern.
quotes.c: Heaven as watcher in Christian cosmology.

quotes.a: The adjective vaulting suggests a rider leaping onto a horse and overshooting. It shows ambition as reckless and unsupported, and Macbeth's own metaphor predicts his fall. The alliterative v sound makes the phrase sound almost proud even as it condemns him.

The conditional and the repeated done create circular thought. The monosyllables sound like a man talking himself round a problem, and the vague word it avoids naming murder. The opening shows his reluctance and the euphemism of fear.
quotes.q: If it were done when 'tis done

quotes.a: Macbeth recognises the vision as imaginary, but the phrase also shows that his mind has become the source of violence. It could suggest the supernatural manipulates him, or that guilt makes his imagination a weapon.
quotes.c: Evil spirits were believed to deceive the mind.

quotes.a: Macbeth now wants security. The adverb safely changes the meaning of being king: it is not power he lacks, but peace. The contrast between thus and safely in a single line shows that crime cannot bring the peace he sought.

Macbeth resolves to turn every impulse into action. It suggests he has abandoned deliberation and moral thought, becoming an agent of impulsive violence. The language is blunt, with none of the imaginative doubt of 1.7.
quotes.c: The tyrant as a ruler of impulse.

quotes.a: The short opening line leaves a silent beat for the news of Lady Macbeth's death. The phrase is unemotional, a mixture of grief and exhaustion. It could suggest he has no energy left for sorrow, or that the timing of events has become meaningless to him.
quotes.c: Time in a world without order.

quotes.a: The alliteration of f and the sibilance create a noisy, hollow sound that fits the idea of a life that means nothing. The phrase suggests that ambition, violence and power are performance without purpose, and it is the last stage of the theatrical imagery that began in 1.3.
quotes.ref: Act 5 Sc 5, closing lines of the soliloquy

quotes.a: She uses a nursing image to describe Macbeth's weakness. Kindness is feminine and nourishing in her mind, but too much of it prevents action. It reveals her view that ruthlessness is necessary, and ironically it connects to the motif of babies and milk later in the play.

summary: Soliloquies and asides give the audience direct access to Macbeth's and Lady Macbeth's thoughts, while dramatic irony places us ahead of characters who do not know what we know. Together they create sympathy, complicity and tragic tension.

terms.d: A speech by a character alone on stage, revealing private thoughts to the audience.
A remark to the audience or to oneself that other characters on stage are supposed not to hear.
When the audience knows something that the characters do not, giving words a second meaning.
A character of high status whose downfall is caused by a flaw and who gains the audience's pity and fear.
The tragic flaw or error of judgement that leads to the hero's downfall.
Excessive pride or ambition that defies natural or divine order.
A question asked for effect rather than to receive an answer.
Addressing an absent person or non-human thing as if it could hear.
A pause or break within a line of verse, often shown by punctuation.
